analogy.p: Think of the food an animal eats as water poured into a bucket full of holes. The water that stays in the bucket is the growth (the meat we can eat); the water that leaks out the holes is energy lost as heat from movement and keeping warm, and as waste. Intensive farming plugs some of the holes by limiting movement and keeping the animal warm, so more of the water stays in. The analogy breaks down because an animal's 'holes' cannot all be blocked: respiration is essential for life, and plugging the holes this way raises animal welfare issues that a bucket does not have.

bullets: **Food security** = having enough food to feed a population (the exact AQA wording to learn).
It is not only about quantity: food must also be available, affordable and nutritious, but the spec definition focuses on having enough.
A population has food security when food production plus imports at least match what people need.
Food insecurity can lead to malnutrition, famine, ill health and conflict, so it is a major global issue.
Farming has to find **sustainable** methods: ones that meet today's needs without damaging the environment so that future generations can still feed themselves.
Link: this topic is the Biology-only ecology 'human use of the biosphere' content; it connects to biodiversity, food webs and trophic levels.
core.p: **Food security** means having enough food to feed a population. It applies to a whole country or region, not just one family, and it is about reliable access to enough safe, nutritious food all of the time. The human population is still growing, so the amount of food produced must keep rising, and it must be produced in ways that can carry on for the long term. Examiners expect a one-line definition, then the ability to link a given factor to a reduced food supply.

bullets: More people means greater demand for food, water and land.
Farmland is a limited resource: building homes on farmland reduces the area available to grow crops.
Where population growth outpaces food production, each person has less food available, leading to hunger.
To cope, yields per hectare must increase or more efficient farming must be used.
Do not just write 'more people': link it to food needed versus food available.
Link: population growth also increases waste, pollution and habitat loss (biodiversity topic).
core.p: In some countries the birth rate is increasing faster than food production can increase, so there are more mouths to feed from the same area of farmland. This threatens food security because the demand for food rises while the supply stays the same or rises more slowly. The spec says that the increasing birth rate has threatened food security in some countries, so remember it is 'some countries' and not every country.

bullets: Eating more meat increases demand: it takes much more land and crop to produce a kilogram of meat than a kilogram of plant food, because energy is lost at each trophic level.
Food transported long distances ('food miles') burns fossil fuels, releasing carbon dioxide and adding to climate change.
Climate change in turn threatens food production elsewhere: a feedback that makes things worse.
Scarce foods being exported can raise prices in the producing country, making food less affordable for local people.
Examiners reward linking the diet change to transport AND the effect on supply.
Link: efficiency of energy transfer through food chains (see later section).
core.h: Factor 2: changing diets in wealthy countries
core.p: In developed (wealthy) countries people's diets have changed so that they now expect to eat foods that are out of season or only grow in distant countries, such as exotic fruit and large amounts of meat. This means scarce food resources are transported around the world, which uses fuel and can leave less food for people in the countries where it was grown. The spec phrase is 'changing diets in some parts of the world means scarce food resources are transported around the world'.

bullets: Pests eat or damage crops directly, lowering yield.
Pathogens cause disease in crops (for example potato blight, a fungus-like pathogen) and in animals (for example foot and mouth disease), reducing the food produced.
Pests and pathogens can evolve resistance to pesticides, fungicides and antibiotics through natural selection, so old controls stop working.
Global trade moves organisms to new places where there are no natural predators.
A monoculture is genetically uniform, so one pathogen can affect every plant.
Control methods include pesticides, crop rotation, biological control and breeding or genetically engineering resistant crops.
core.p: New **pests** (such as insects that eat crops) and new **pathogens** (such as fungi, bacteria and viruses that cause plant or animal disease) can damage or destroy crops and livestock. They may be introduced by global trade and travel, or may evolve resistance to existing pesticides and treatments. Because farms often grow large areas of a single crop (monoculture), a new disease can spread quickly and wipe out huge quantities of food.

bullets: Failed rains cause drought: crops wilt, yields fall and famine can follow in areas relying on rain-fed farming.
Flooding can wash away soil and drown crops.
Climate change (caused partly by greenhouse gases) is making weather patterns less predictable.
Soil erosion and loss of fertile soil reduce the land available for farming.
Rising sea level can flood coastal farmland with salt water.
Link: global warming (4.7.3.2) and deforestation affect the same issues.
core.p: Environmental changes that affect food production include drought, flooding, rising temperatures and unpredictable weather. The spec example is widespread famine occurring in some countries if rains fail. Crops need water, suitable temperatures and light for photosynthesis, so changes in these directly reduce crop yield and the growth of livestock.

bullets: High cost of fertiliser or seed means lower yields or less land planted.
Rising fuel prices make machinery and transport more expensive, so food prices rise.
War can destroy crops, irrigation and storage, and block food aid.
Conflict over shared rivers or water can leave farms with too little water.
Remember all six spec factors: birth rate, changing diets, new pests and pathogens, environmental change, cost of inputs, conflict.
In a 'name' question, one-word answers are weak: add a short effect such as 'so less food is produced'.
core.p: Two further factors are the cost of agricultural inputs and conflicts that affect the availability of water or food. Inputs are the things a farmer must buy, such as seed, fertiliser, pesticides, animal feed and fuel. If these become too expensive, farmers (especially in poorer countries) cannot afford them, so they produce less food. Conflict destroys farmland, disrupts transport and markets, forces people to flee, and can be used to cut off water supplies.

bullets: Only a small part of the energy in feed ends up as biomass in the animal; the rest is lost as heat from respiration and as waste.
Efficiency = (biomass transferred ÷ biomass available) × 100.
Two spec methods: **limit the animal's movement** and **control the temperature of its surroundings**.
Less movement means less energy released by respiration for muscle contraction.
A warm environment means less energy is needed to maintain body temperature, because less heat is lost to the surroundings.
The saved energy is used for growth, so the animal reaches market size faster on less feed.
Higher tier link: biomass transfer calculations use the same efficiency formula.
core.p: Sustainable ways must be found to feed all the people on Earth. One approach is to improve the **efficiency of food production** by reducing the energy lost from food animals to the environment. Energy that an animal takes in as food is used in respiration (for movement and to keep body temperature), is lost in waste, or is stored as new biomass that humans can eat. The more energy that goes into growth rather than being lost, the more food is produced from the same amount of feed.

bullets: Movement limited by pens, cages or crates, so less respiration for movement.
Temperature controlled with heating, insulation and ventilation, so less energy used for keeping warm.
Feeding is controlled, giving high-energy feed so animals grow quickly.
Animals protected from predators and many diseases, so fewer losses.
Result: higher yield (more meat per unit of feed), lower cost and cheaper food, which supports food security.
Often called 'factory farming' or intensive farming: a term to recognise but explain in terms of energy.
core.h: Intensive animal farming: how it works
core.p: Raising animals indoors in pens or cages (for example broiler chickens in sheds or pigs in stalls) is an example of this restricted movement and controlled temperature. Because the animals cannot roam and the shed is kept warm, more of the energy in their food goes into growth. Fewer animals die from predators or cold, and disease and feeding can be closely controlled, so more food is produced from less feed, land and time.

bullets: Advantage: more food from less feed and land, lower prices, helps feed a growing population.
Disadvantage: animal welfare concerns: restricted movement and crowded conditions.
Crowding spreads disease, so antibiotics are used routinely; this can increase antibiotic resistance.
Large amounts of waste (slurry) can pollute water if not managed, and housing uses energy.
Balanced answers use phrases like 'on the one hand... on the other hand' and finish with a judgement.
Do not write 'it is cruel' alone: say which welfare problem (movement, space) and what its effect is.
core.h: Evaluating intensive farming: ethics and the environment
core.p: Examiners often ask you to evaluate or discuss intensive animal farming. The benefits are higher efficiency and cheaper food, but there are ethical and practical concerns. Many people believe it is cruel for animals to be kept in cramped conditions with little freedom to carry out natural behaviours, so animal welfare is a major ethical objection. Crowding also makes disease spread faster, which can lead to heavy use of antibiotics and the evolution of antibiotic-resistant bacteria.

bullets: **Net size (mesh size)**: nets with larger holes let young, small fish escape.
Escaped juveniles can grow to adult size and breed, replacing the fish that are caught.
**Fishing quotas** limit the mass or number of fish of each species that boats may land in a given time.
Quotas stop the population being fished faster than it reproduces, so stocks can recover.
Other measures include banning fishing in breeding grounds or seasons (a wider idea; do not rely on it in place of net size and quotas).
Overfishing also disrupts food webs because predators and prey are affected.
core.p: Some people get food from the fish stocks in the oceans. Overfishing, taking fish faster than they can reproduce, reduces the stock and can cause a population collapse. Fish stocks must therefore be kept at a **sustainable level**, which means the number of fish caught should not be more than the number that are replaced by breeding. The spec names two ways of conserving fish stocks: net size and fishing quotas.

bullets: International waters are hard to police, so illegal fishing can occur.
Setting a quota needs good data on stock size and breeding rate, which is hard to measure.
Small catch limits may hit the livelihoods of fishing communities, creating economic arguments against conservation.
Bycatch (unwanted species caught by accident) can threaten other species.
Sustainable = harvested no faster than the stock can replace itself.
Answers should show that conservation protects both biodiversity and the long-term food supply.
core.p: Fish stocks are difficult to conserve because the oceans are shared and boats can be hard to monitor. Quotas depend on accurate scientific data about the size of the population, and fishing fleets and countries compete for the same fish. Stricter rules can reduce the income and jobs of fishing communities, so there is a conflict between short-term economic needs and long-term sustainability.

bullets: Biomass is lost between trophic levels through respiration, movement, heat, excretion, and parts that are not eaten (bones, roots).
If 10 000 kJ is in plants, only about 1 000 kJ is in the herbivore and about 100 kJ in the next carnivore.
Growing crops for humans uses land more efficiently than feeding crops to animals first.
This is why changing diets to include a lot of meat puts more pressure on food security.
Calculation: percentage efficiency = (biomass transferred ÷ biomass at previous level) × 100.
Higher tier: be ready to calculate and interpret biomass efficiency from data.
core.h: Efficiency and food chains: why diet matters
core.p: At each trophic level only about 10% of the biomass is transferred to the next level; most is lost as waste, in respiration and as inedible parts. This is why food chains are rarely longer than four or five trophic levels and why eating plants directly supplies more usable energy per hectare than eating animals fed on those plants. Reducing the number of steps between producer and human is therefore a way of improving the efficiency of food production.

bullets: Quote data with units when describing a trend, and calculate changes or percentages if asked.
A falling fish catch despite constant fishing effort suggests the stock has been overfished.
Compare two farming methods using efficiency = biomass gained ÷ food eaten × 100.
Evaluate: weigh benefits (more food, lower cost) against drawbacks (welfare, antibiotic resistance, pollution).
Use the command words correctly: 'Explain' = give reasons; 'Evaluate' = weigh up and conclude; 'Suggest' = apply knowledge to a new context.
Link to other topics: trophic levels, respiration, natural selection (resistance), biodiversity and climate change.
core.h: Interpreting data and evaluating on food security
core.p: Questions on this topic often give you data (for example a table of the mass of feed eaten and the mass gained, or a graph of fish catches over time) and ask you to interpret or evaluate it. Use figures in your answer, calculate efficiency where you can, and link the pattern to the biology. For long answers, structure your response: state the issue, give biological reasons, give the advantages, give the drawbacks and then reach a justified conclusion.

exam: Define 'food security' in one line: 'having enough food to feed a population' (1 mark).
'Give/State' questions for factors (1 mark each): name one of the six factors and add the effect, for example 'new pests destroying crops, so less food is produced'.
'Explain why' (2 to 3 marks): use 'because' chains: less movement, so less respiration, so less energy lost as heat, so more energy used for growth.
Always say energy is 'lost to the surroundings as heat' or 'in waste', never that it is 'used up'.
For fish: net size and quotas each earn a mark if you say what they do AND why it helps the stock recover (juveniles breed; limited catch).

6-mark evaluate questions: give at least two advantages, two disadvantages (ethical, environmental, economic) and a final justified conclusion; use the indicative-content level descriptors in mind (linked reasoning scores top).
Calculation questions: show the working. Efficiency = biomass gained ÷ biomass in feed × 100, and give a unit (%).
Graph or table questions: quote values with units, state the trend, then give the biological reason.
'Suggest' questions: apply what you know to the new situation given; one valid idea with a reason is enough per mark.
Do not just write 'cruel': link animal welfare to a feature such as cramped space or inability to move freely.
Avoid vague words: 'more food' is weaker than 'higher yield per hectare' or 'more biomass per kg of feed'.

mistakes.r: Food security is having enough food to feed a population.
mistakes.w: Food security means everyone is rich enough to buy food.

mistakes.r: They use less energy in movement and keeping warm, so more energy from food goes into growth (biomass).
mistakes.w: Animals in cages grow faster because they are happier.

mistakes.r: Energy is transferred to the surroundings as heat (and in waste); it is not destroyed.
mistakes.w: Animals use up energy and it disappears.

mistakes.r: Larger mesh lets smaller, younger fish escape so they can grow and breed, keeping the stock sustainable.
A quota limits the amount of each species that can be caught, so the population is not fished faster than it reproduces.
mistakes.w: A quota means nobody can fish.

mistakes.r: State a specific issue: welfare (restricted movement), disease spread and antibiotic use, or pollution from waste.
mistakes.w: Intensive farming is bad because it is unnatural (no biology given).

mistakes.r: About 10% of the biomass is transferred to the next level; the rest is lost as waste, in respiration and in uneaten parts.
mistakes.w: Only about 10% of the plants are eaten, so 90% of the plants are wasted.

mistakes.r: Pests are organisms (often insects) that damage crops; pathogens are microorganisms that cause disease.
mistakes.w: Pests and pathogens are the same thing.

summary: AQA Biology only (4.7.3.4): you must know what food security is, the biological and other factors that threaten it, and how food production can be made more efficient by reducing energy transfer from food animals to the environment (limiting movement and controlling temperature), plus how net size and fishing quotas conserve fish stocks. It matters because exam questions ask you to explain, evaluate and weigh up the benefits against the ethical and environmental costs.

terms.d: Having enough food to feed a population.
Meeting present needs without damaging the environment or reducing the ability of future generations to meet their needs.
An organism, such as an insect, that damages crops or livestock and reduces food production.
Growing a single crop over a large area, so all plants are genetically similar and vulnerable to the same pest or disease.
The mass of living material (usually dry mass) in organisms or a trophic level.
A feeding level in a food chain, for example producer, primary consumer, secondary consumer.
The proportion of the energy or biomass in the food supplied that ends up as useful biomass; it can be increased by reducing energy losses.
Farming that aims to maximise yield from a small area, for example animals kept indoors with restricted movement and controlled temperature.
The chemical reaction that transfers energy from glucose to living cells; some energy is lost as heat to the surroundings.
The population of a particular species of fish in an area of sea that is harvested by people.
A limit on the quantity of a species of fish that may be caught in a given period.
The size of the holes in a fishing net; larger holes let young fish escape.
Catching fish faster than the population can reproduce, so the stock declines.
Protecting and managing species and habitats so that populations are maintained at a sustainable level.
Widespread, extreme shortage of food in a region that causes hunger, illness and death.
Where bacteria are no longer killed by an antibiotic because resistant strains have survived and reproduced.

worked.ans: Roaming 10%, barn 14%; the barn calves gain 40% more biomass from the same feed.
worked.q: A farmer feeds calves 4000 kg dry mass of feed. Calves free to roam gain 400 kg dry mass of biomass; calves in a warm barn gain 560 kg from the same feed. Calculate the efficiency for each and the percentage increase in biomass gained. (4 marks)

worked.ans: Limited movement and a warm environment reduce the energy lost to the surroundings through respiration, so more energy goes into growth and more meat is produced from the same food.
worked.q: Explain how limiting the movement of food animals and keeping them warm increases the efficiency of food production. (3 marks)
steps: Less movement means less energy is transferred by respiration for muscle contraction (1).
A warm environment means less energy is needed to maintain body temperature, so less heat is lost to the surroundings (1).
More of the energy in the food is therefore used for growth, producing more biomass (1).

worked.ans: Larger mesh lets young fish escape and breed, and quotas limit the catch, so fewer fish are removed than are replaced by reproduction and the stock remains sustainable.
worked.q: A fishing company is concerned about falling catches. Explain how using nets with larger holes and fishing quotas could help keep the fish stock at a sustainable level. (4 marks)
steps: Larger holes allow young (juvenile) fish to escape the net (1).
The escaped fish grow to maturity and breed, replacing the fish that are caught (1).
A quota limits the number or mass of fish that can be caught (1).
So fish are not removed faster than they reproduce and the population can recover or stay stable (1).
